questions.stem: Why is the performance of staff closely linked to achieving business objectives?
options: Staff performance affects only labour costs and has no link to sales or reputation.
Staff performance matters only in large businesses that employ hundreds of people.
Staff carry out the work that produces goods, serves customers and generates sales.
Staff set the business's objectives, which managers must then follow without change.
questions.explanation: Staff are the people who make products, serve customers and carry out the business's plans, so their productivity and quality of work directly affect objectives such as profit and customer satisfaction. This applies to businesses of every size.

questions.stem: A new Ballarat café has the objective of an average customer rating of 4.5 stars. Which staffing decision most directly supports this objective?
options: employing fewer staff during busy periods so that each shift is cheaper
allowing staff to choose their own service standards on each shift
hiring staff with strong customer service skills and training them well
hiring the cheapest available staff to keep the café's wage costs low
questions.explanation: Customer ratings depend on the service customers receive, so skilled, well-trained staff are central to this objective. Cutting staff numbers or costs at busy times is likely to cause long waits and lower ratings.

questions.stem: When identifying its staffing needs, a new business should consider:
options: the knowledge, skills and ideas that staff can contribute
only the lowest wage it is legally allowed to pay staff
only the number of staff its competitors currently employ
only the personal preferences of the owner's friends
questions.explanation: Identifying staffing needs means working out how many staff are needed and what knowledge, skills and ideas they must bring to meet the business's objectives. Wages and competitors' staffing may be relevant, but neither alone identifies the business's needs.

questions.stem: A planned Geelong landscaping business expects heavy demand in spring and summer but little work in winter. Its staffing plan should most likely include:
options: permanent part-time staff who must work their highest hours in winter
a small core of permanent staff, with casual staff added in peak seasons
a large permanent full-time workforce that is employed all year round
no employees at all, with the owner doing all of the work in every season
questions.explanation: Matching staff numbers to seasonal demand keeps labour costs under control while still meeting peak workloads. A large permanent workforce would be paid through winter when there is little work.

questions.stem: A new Perth supermarket installs self-service checkouts. The most likely effect on its staffing needs is:
options: more checkout operators, because customers will need help at every one of the self-service machines
no further need for any staff, because the checkouts can run the store unassisted
a need to hire only qualified software engineers to replace all of the store's staff
fewer checkout operators, but a need for staff who can assist customers and fix machines
questions.explanation: Automation usually reduces the number of staff needed for routine tasks but creates demand for staff with different skills, such as supporting customers and maintaining equipment. The store still needs staff for many other tasks.

questions.stem: A Hobart accounting firm adopts cloud software that automates much of its data entry. Which staffing response best balances the firm's objectives and its staff?
options: keep staff on the same tasks, as the software cannot perform data entry
stop hiring accountants, because the software will advise clients itself
retrain data-entry staff for advisory roles that now have more demand
dismiss all data-entry staff without notice, since the work is now done
questions.explanation: Retraining keeps staff whose knowledge of the firm is valuable and moves them into higher-value work created by the technology. Dismissing staff without notice would breach the National Employment Standards on notice of termination.

questions.stem: Job analysis is:
options: the process of interviewing each of the applicants to decide who should be offered the job
a review of an existing employee's performance against the goals set for them
the process of advertising a vacant job on websites and social media platforms
a systematic study of a job to identify its tasks and the skills needed to perform it
questions.explanation: Job analysis examines what a job involves and what it requires, providing the information used to design the job and write its job description and job specification. Interviewing applicants is part of selection, which comes later.

questions.stem: A job description sets out:
options: the steps used to select the best job applicant
the induction program for the new employee
the tasks, duties and responsibilities of the job
the qualifications and personal qualities required
questions.explanation: A job description describes the job itself: its tasks, duties, responsibilities and who the role reports to. The qualifications and personal qualities required of the person are listed in the job specification.

questions.stem: An advertisement for a Bendigo pharmacy assistant requires 'a Certificate III in Community Pharmacy, strong communication skills and a friendly manner'. This information comes from the:
options: job specification
job description
employment contract
induction handbook
questions.explanation: A job specification lists the qualifications, skills, experience and personal attributes a person needs to do the job. A job description lists the duties of the role rather than the qualities of the person.

questions.stem: Which sequence best shows the relationship between job analysis and other staffing documents?
options: job description, then job analysis, then the job specification and job design
job specification, then recruitment, then job analysis and the job description
recruitment, then job analysis, then job design and the job specification
job analysis, then job design, then the job description and job specification
questions.explanation: Job analysis gathers information about the job, which is used to design the job and then to write the job description and specification. These documents come before recruitment, because they define what the business is recruiting for.

questions.stem: Job design involves:
options: deciding which tasks make up a job and how they are organised
choosing the most suitable applicant from all of those who applied
writing the advertisement that will attract job applicants
setting the minimum wage that will be paid for the role
questions.explanation: Job design determines the content of a job, such as which tasks it includes and how much variety and responsibility it has. Choosing between applicants is selection, and minimum wages are set through the Fair Work system.

questions.stem: Which is an internal recruitment method?
options: posting the vacancy on a public online job website
engaging an online recruitment agency
promoting the vacancy on public social media
advertising the vacancy on the business's intranet
questions.explanation: Internal recruitment seeks applicants from among existing staff, for example through the intranet or word of mouth within the business. Job websites, recruitment agencies and public social media reach people outside the business.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of internal recruitment compared with external recruitment?
options: It is usually cheaper and faster, and the applicants' performance is already known.
It brings a much wider range of applicants with new skills and ideas into the business.
It never creates a further vacancy that must then be filled elsewhere.
It guarantees that no existing employee will be disappointed by the outcome.
questions.explanation: Recruiting internally saves advertising costs and time, and managers already know the applicants' work. A wider pool with fresh ideas is the main advantage of external recruitment, and promoting someone internally leaves their old role vacant.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of filling vacancies by word of mouth is that it:
options: is the most expensive recruitment method available to small businesses
is not allowed under Australian equal employment opportunity laws
always attracts far too many applicants for the business to assess
may limit the pool of applicants and reduce diversity in the workforce
questions.explanation: Word of mouth reaches only people connected to current staff, so the pool of applicants is small and may lack variety. It is usually very cheap, which is why small businesses often use it.

questions.stem: A new Melbourne design studio advertises a vacancy on social media. Which is a likely advantage of this method?
options: It is an internal method that limits applicants to current staff.
It removes any need for a selection process for the job.
It can reach many potential applicants quickly and at low cost.
It guarantees that only qualified applicants will apply.
questions.explanation: Social media can spread a job advertisement widely and quickly, often for little cost, and can target people with particular interests. It may also attract many unsuitable applicants who must then be screened.

questions.stem: A Sunshine Coast hotel needs an experienced chef urgently and has no suitable internal candidates. Which recruitment method is most appropriate, and why?
options: waiting for applicants to approach the hotel, which costs nothing and is quickest
an online recruitment agency, which can quickly find skilled candidates from a wide pool
the hotel's intranet, which will reach current staff who are not trained chefs
word of mouth among existing staff, which guarantees a wide and diverse pool of chefs
questions.explanation: When no internal candidate has the skills, an external method is needed, and a recruitment agency can search a wide pool and shortlist experienced candidates quickly. Agencies charge fees, but the urgency and skill level justify the cost.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares online recruitment agencies with the business's own careers website?
options: Agencies are always cheaper, while a careers website always attracts a much larger and more skilled pool of applicants.
Both are internal recruitment methods, so neither will reach any applicants from outside the business.
A careers website screens applicants automatically, so agencies are only needed by government bodies.
Agencies reach a wider pool and screen applicants but charge fees; the website is cheaper but reaches fewer people.
questions.explanation: Recruitment agencies have large databases and handle screening, which saves time but adds cost. A careers website costs little but mainly reaches people who already know of the business and visit its site.

questions.stem: Which is a selection method?
options: work testing
word of mouth
job analysis
induction
questions.explanation: Selection methods, such as interviews, psychological testing, work testing and online selection, are used to choose between applicants. Word of mouth is a recruitment method, and job analysis and induction come before and after selection.

questions.stem: Applicants for a barista role at a new Fremantle café are each asked to make three coffees during a busy period. Which is the main advantage of this selection method?
options: It reveals each applicant's personality traits and attitudes to work in great depth.
It is the cheapest and fastest way to assess a very large number of applicants.
It removes any need to check applicants' references or employment histories.
It shows directly whether applicants have the practical skills the job requires.
questions.explanation: A work test assesses actual performance on tasks from the job, giving strong evidence of practical skill. It takes time to run for each applicant and does not test every quality, such as reliability over months.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of the interview as a selection method is that:
options: it gives no information about applicants' communication
it cannot be used for any job that involves customers
it is not permitted under the National Employment Standards
an interviewer's personal bias may affect the decision
questions.explanation: Interviews can be subjective: interviewers may favour applicants who are similar to them or who interview well but perform poorly. Interviews do give useful information about communication and attitude, which is why they are widely used.

questions.stem: A large retailer asks applicants to complete an online personality and aptitude questionnaire. This selection method is:
options: psychological testing
work testing
a reference check
a panel interview
questions.explanation: Psychological tests measure characteristics such as personality, aptitude and reasoning. Work testing would instead have applicants perform real tasks from the job.

questions.stem: A national retailer receives 3,000 applications for 50 casual roles and uses online screening to shortlist applicants automatically. Which evaluation is most valid?
options: It saves time with large numbers, but it may wrongly screen out suitable applicants.
It is always fairer than interviews, because online screening tools cannot contain any bias.
It removes any need for later interviews or work tests for the roles being filled.
It is unsuitable, because online selection cannot be used for casual positions.
questions.explanation: Online selection is efficient when applications are numerous, but automated filters can reject good applicants whose answers do not match expected keywords, and can reflect biases in how they were set up. It works best combined with other methods.

questions.stem: The National Employment Standards (NES) are:
options: rules made by individual employers and written into each of their own staff handbooks
minimum employment entitlements that apply to employees in the national workplace relations system
voluntary guidelines on good workplace practice that employers may adopt or ignore if they choose
the rates of pay that every award sets for each type of job in a particular industry
questions.explanation: The NES, set out in the Fair Work Act 2009, are minimum entitlements that cannot be reduced by an award, agreement or contract. Rates of pay are set in awards, agreements and the national minimum wage, not in the NES.

questions.stem: Under the National Employment Standards, a full-time employee is entitled to:
options: four weeks of paid annual leave for each year of service
six weeks of paid annual leave for each year of service
two weeks of paid annual leave for each year of service
unlimited paid annual leave once they have 12 months' service
questions.explanation: The NES give full-time employees four weeks of paid annual leave a year, with part-time employees receiving a pro-rata amount. Some shift workers receive an additional week.

questions.stem: Under the National Employment Standards, the maximum weekly hours for a full-time employee are:
options: 35 hours, plus unlimited additional hours
45 hours, plus reasonable additional hours
38 hours, plus reasonable additional hours
40 hours, with no additional hours ever allowed
questions.explanation: The NES set maximum weekly hours of 38 for full-time employees, and an employer may ask for reasonable additional hours. Whether extra hours are reasonable depends on factors such as the employee's health, family responsibilities and the notice given.

questions.stem: Which is an entitlement under the National Employment Standards?
options: a company car for every full-time manager
paid personal/carer's leave for permanent employees
a guaranteed annual pay rise in line with inflation
paid annual leave for all casual employees
questions.explanation: Permanent employees accrue paid personal/carer's leave under the NES, which they can use when sick or caring for a family member. Casual employees receive a higher hourly rate instead of paid annual and personal leave, and pay rises are not an NES entitlement.

questions.stem: Under the National Employment Standards, how much notice must an employer give when dismissing an employee aged 50 who has four years of continuous service, other than for serious misconduct?
options: 5 weeks
4 weeks
3 weeks
2 weeks
questions.explanation: An employee with more than three and up to five years of service is entitled to three weeks' notice, and an employee over 45 with at least two years' service gets one extra week, making four weeks. Forgetting the extra week for age gives three weeks.

questions.stem: A contract of employment is:
options: a government licence that a business needs before it can hire any employees
a record of the training that an employee has completed since starting work
an agreement setting out the terms and conditions between an employer and an employee
a document listing the qualifications that a job applicant must hold before they apply
questions.explanation: A contract of employment, written or verbal, sets out terms such as duties, hours, pay and conditions. It cannot provide less than the NES and any applicable award or agreement.

questions.stem: An employer's expectation of loyalty from employees most likely includes:
options: refusing to join a trade union or any other association
keeping the business's confidential information private
working unlimited unpaid overtime whenever it is requested
never taking any of their annual leave entitlement
questions.explanation: Employers expect loyal employees to act in the business's interests, for example by protecting confidential information and not helping competitors. Employees cannot be required to give up legal entitlements such as annual leave, and they have a right to join a union.

questions.stem: An employee at a Geelong engineering firm resigns and leaves the next day, although her contract requires two weeks' notice. Which employer expectation has she failed to meet?
options: remuneration
terms of notice
work-life balance
job security
questions.explanation: Employers expect employees to give the notice set out in their contract or award, so that the business has time to arrange cover or a replacement. Work-life balance, job security and remuneration are expectations that employees hold of employers.

questions.stem: Which is an employee expectation of an employer?
options: loyalty to the business
terms of notice on resignation
a signed contract of employment
job security
questions.explanation: Employees expect job security, fair remuneration, good conditions of employment and a reasonable work-life balance. Loyalty and proper notice on resignation are expectations employers have of their employees.

questions.stem: A software developer accepts a lower salary at a new Canberra firm because it offers flexible hours and the option to work from home. She is giving priority to:
options: work-life balance
job security
terms of notice
loyalty
questions.explanation: Choosing flexibility over higher pay shows that she values work-life balance, the ability to manage work alongside her personal life. Job security concerns how safe her ongoing employment is, which the scenario does not mention.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares employer and employee expectations about notice and loyalty?
options: Employees expect loyalty from employers, while employers expect employees to give no notice at all when leaving.
Only employers have expectations, because employee expectations are fully covered by the NES.
Both expect the same thing, so contracts of employment are not needed in small businesses.
Employers expect loyalty and proper notice; employees expect job security and fair treatment in return.
questions.explanation: The employment relationship involves obligations on both sides: employers want commitment and adequate notice, and employees want secure jobs, fair pay and good conditions. Expectations such as work-life balance go beyond the legal minimum in the NES.

questions.stem: Under Victoria's Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004, employers must:
options: guarantee that no accident or injury of any kind will ever happen in the workplace, whatever the cost or the circumstances
pay every employee a safety bonus each year in which no injuries are reported anywhere in the workplace
leave all responsibility for workplace safety to employees, who must manage their own risks independently
provide and maintain a working environment that is safe and without risks to health, so far as is reasonably practicable
questions.explanation: The Act places a duty on employers to provide a safe workplace so far as is reasonably practicable, including safe equipment, systems of work, training and supervision. No law can guarantee that accidents will never occur, and employees also have duties of their own.

questions.stem: Under OH&S law, an employee of a new Dandenong warehouse must:
options: obtain WorkCover insurance in their own name
take reasonable care for their own safety and the safety of others
pay for their own safety equipment out of their wages
take sole responsibility for the safety of everyone in the warehouse
questions.explanation: Employees must take reasonable care for their own health and safety and that of others, and cooperate with their employer's safety measures. Providing safety equipment and holding WorkCover insurance are the employer's responsibilities.

questions.stem: Equal employment opportunity (EEO) legislation requires that staffing decisions be made:
options: only after every applicant has completed a psychological test
on the basis of who will accept the lowest rate of pay for the job
on merit, without discrimination based on attributes such as age, sex or race
in favour of applicants who are already known personally to current staff members
questions.explanation: EEO laws, such as Victoria's Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and federal anti-discrimination Acts, prohibit discrimination on protected attributes in recruitment, selection, pay and promotion. Decisions must be based on the ability to do the job.

questions.stem: The owner of a new Shepparton fitness studio decides not to interview a well-qualified applicant because she is 52, believing younger trainers will appeal more to customers. Which statement is correct?
options: This breaches the OH&S Act, because the decision affects workplace safety.
This is likely to be unlawful age discrimination under equal opportunity law.
This is lawful, because a business may consider what its own customers prefer.
This is lawful, as long as the business has fewer than 20 employees.
questions.explanation: Refusing to consider an applicant because of her age, when she can do the job, is discrimination on a protected attribute under equal opportunity laws. Customer preferences do not justify discrimination, and the decision is an EEO matter, not a safety one.

questions.stem: The main purpose of employee induction is to:
options: help new staff become familiar with the business and productive quickly
choose the most suitable applicant from a shortlist of candidates
assess whether existing staff have met the annual performance goals set for them
advertise new vacancies to people working outside the business
questions.explanation: Induction introduces new employees to the workplace, their colleagues, policies, procedures and safety requirements, so they settle in and become productive sooner. Choosing between applicants is selection, which comes before induction.

questions.stem: On his first day at a new Bendigo hardware store, a new employee tours the store, meets his team and is shown the emergency exits and safety procedures. This is:
options: induction
recruitment
selection
job analysis
questions.explanation: Showing a new employee around the workplace, introducing colleagues and explaining safety procedures are typical induction activities. Recruitment and selection happen before the person starts work.

questions.stem: Which is a common method of employee induction?
options: requiring the new employee to sit a psychological test
advertising the employee's previous role on the intranet
asking the new employee to write their own job description
assigning a buddy or mentor to support the new employee
questions.explanation: Buddy or mentor systems, orientation tours, handbooks, information sessions and online modules are common induction methods. Psychological tests are a selection method used before an offer is made.

questions.stem: A new Brisbane call centre gives its staff no induction, and many leave within their first month. Which is the most likely explanation?
options: A lack of induction always lowers the business's wage costs, which encourages staff to resign.
New staff felt unsupported and unsure of their roles, so they left before settling in.
Induction only matters for safety, so it cannot affect how long staff stay in a job.
The staff left because the business had followed the National Employment Standards.
questions.explanation: Without induction, new staff may not understand their role, the culture or where to get help, which increases stress and early resignations. Good induction improves retention as well as safety and productivity.

questions.stem: A new Mildura farm recruits fruit pickers from overseas. Which action best reflects corporate social responsibility?
options: paying overseas workers less than the award, since their wages are worth more at home
holding the workers' passports so that they cannot leave before the season ends
charging the workers high fees for accommodation to recover the recruitment costs
ensuring overseas workers receive the same pay and conditions as Australian workers
questions.explanation: Socially responsible employers treat overseas workers fairly, giving them at least their legal entitlements and safe conditions. Underpaying workers or holding their passports is exploitation and is unlawful.

questions.stem: Which staffing decision best reflects corporate social responsibility when a business is being established?
options: choosing staff based mainly on who will accept the lowest pay for the role
recruiting only from the owner's own friends to save on advertising costs
offering traineeships to young local people facing barriers to work
hiring only casual staff so that no one ever accrues leave entitlements
questions.explanation: CSR in staffing goes beyond legal minimums, for example by creating opportunities for disadvantaged people or building a diverse workforce. Structuring jobs to avoid entitlements or paying the least possible puts cost ahead of staff wellbeing.

questions.stem: A new Darwin construction firm can fill skilled roles faster by recruiting from overseas than by training local apprentices. Which evaluation best reflects CSR considerations?
options: Overseas recruitment is always irresponsible, so the firm should leave the roles vacant until local people are trained.
Training local apprentices has no social benefit, so the firm should rely entirely on overseas recruitment.
CSR does not apply to recruitment, so the firm should simply choose whichever option costs least.
Overseas recruitment fills skill gaps, but the firm should treat those workers fairly and also train local people.
questions.explanation: A responsible approach can combine overseas recruitment for urgent skill needs with fair treatment of those workers and investment in local training. CSR applies to staffing decisions, including who is recruited and how they are treated.
